Oṃ. [Now begins the *Anādivīraśaivasārasaṃgraha*].
[First Chapter]

Salutations to the venerable Guru Basava Liṅga. Salutations to the venerable Guru Prabhu. Salutations to the venerable Gaṇeśa. Salutations to the venerable Śiva. Salutations to the venerable Guru. Oṃ, salutations to Sarvamaṅgalā.
May there be well-being for the author of this *Anādivīraśaivasārasaṃgraha*. Oṃ, salutations to the illustrious Lord of the Bull, whose very nature is primordial devotion.
Salutation to the one whose limbs are the eight enclosures of Śiva, who sets in motion the path of the six planes (ṣaṭsthalādhvan). || 1 ||
Victory to Basavarāja, who is worshipped for his bulk and purity,
and whose innate devotion shines forth within the assembly of the hosts of Pramathas!

He who has struck down the suffering of those bowed in devotion, who fulfills the expansive Vedic injunctions, whose fame has reached the firm quarters of the earth, and who is the very embodiment of the Lord Śrī-Vṛṣādhīśa. || 2 ||
The section on the Sūtra of the Pīṭhikā (*Atharvaṇa-śruti*): "Oṃ! Devotion is directly established in Brahman as the mere state of being mounted upon the Bull;
by means of that devotion, its seed-syllable is called the 'Eternal Bull' (*anādi-vṛṣaṇa*)."
Devotion, action, non-desire, and firm conviction are known as the four feet; thus, one who is always oriented toward that Truth is indeed ever-bowed at its head.
The two ears are the uninterrupted internal and external resonance (*nāda*), firm-tipped like the horns of a bull that uproots the sprouts of expectation, indifference,
and ignorance; and the sight is the uninterrupted internal and external vision within the supreme heart.

Thus, the Brahmins who speak of Brahman always declare that the nose is indeed the fragrance of one's own internal impressions of Brahman, which are uninterrupted and extend to the furthest limit; that the tongue is the ever-fresh relish and taste born of that very beginningless longing; and that the rear part [of the body] is the capacity for bearing the burden of carrying forth Brahman, which is speech itself.

Its heart is the support for the crushing of the majesty of the Brahman’s property; its belly is that which has internalized that very [property], like the sky as its own form; its navel is "always going toward Brahman"; its secret organ is "the secret"; its back is indeed the "unworldly state";
and its tail is "always crossing to the further shore by means of its own support."

The ascertainment of the majesty of Brahman is itself the glory of the forehead; thus, the supreme greatness of the nature of the Bull (Dharma) becomes the very essence of Being-Consciousness-Bliss. || 3 ||
You are Dharma in the form of a bull, the bringer of joy to the world.
Therefore, O Eternal One, protect me, for you are the abode of the eightfold form.
Whatever sacred fords exist upon the earth, extending as far as the ocean—those indeed [are there].
They remain perched upon the egg of a bull at the onset of night.
The auspiciousness consisting of salutation to the chosen deity [is attained] by touching the testicles of a bull and beholding Śaṅkara.
The sin committed over seven lifetimes perishes at that very moment.
In the Laingya, the sage said:
And they praised the Lord, the chief of the Gaṇas, the bestower of desired boons, with pleasing words.
Just as the gods, upon seeing his majesty, had their skin bristle with joy.
At the command of the Wielder of the Thunderbolt, the clouds rained down a shower of flowers upon his head.
And the Nandinas showered down a rain rich in fragrance, resonant with the humming of bees.
Touched by the rain, he then shone like one who has been touched with affectionate water.
And Nandibhava was bathed by Adrijayā with fragrant water.
There, the back of the bull shines with various kinds of flowers.
But the surface of the sky was crowded with them, O observers of good vows, like the heavens with stars.
To the one whose mind tastes the nectar of devotion to Śiva, and who is born from Śiva.
Salutation to the illustrious Nandinātha, who is a supreme form of Śaṅkara.
Homage to Basavarāja, whose supreme form is that of the Lord of Bulls.
To him who is solely devoted to the worship of the mobile [deity] and who promotes the conduct of Śiva; || 12 ||
The meter.
Having conquered the succession of crooked machinations of King Bijjala, that foremost of Vīraśaivas swiftly besieged the sun for seven days.
I bow to that supreme deity Vasaveśvara, who is the very form of Paraśiva, who, by means of the "grass-man" (tṛṇapūruṣa) through the vision of consciousness, turned back that Mīmāṃsaka. 13.
Īśvara said:
The letter *va* is the form of the Guru, and the letter *sa* is the Liṅga itself.
The letter *va* is the form of movement (*cara*), and that which is called *basa* is threefold. || 14 ||
The letter *va* is the form of sound (*nāda*), and the letter *sa* is the form of the bindu.
The letter *va* is the form of *kalā*, and the syllable *ba* consists of three colors.
Devotees, liberated souls, and those who are detached [all chant] these three syllables: "Basa-v-eti."
They should always recite it with devotion; it is like a fire to the cotton of one's sins.
O Goddess, he in whose mouth the three syllables "Ba-sa-va" reside—
I dwell there constantly; this is the truth, the truth, and not otherwise. || 17 ||
Salutation to the yogi whose mind tastes the nectar of the principle of Śiva.
Salutations to the illustrious Lord Cannabasava, the proponent of the Brahman of the six stations (ṣaṭsthala).
To the bestower of knowledge upon all the hosts, beginning with Basaveśa.
Salutation to that Lord, the sovereign of yogis, the source of all, whose form is Śiva.
To him whose mental activity is immersed in the ocean of the nectar of Śiva-yoga.
Salutations to the illustrious Siddharāma, who brings joy through the prosperity of his devotees. || 20 ||

The auspicious opening in the form of salutation to the chosen deity [is offered] to the devotees who are content with their own gains, to the virtuous ones, and to those who are the greatest friends of all living beings.
I bow my head repeatedly to those who are free from ego and are peaceful.
In the Śaṅkarasaṃhitā of the Skanda Purāṇa, there is an account.
My child, these leaders of the Gaṇas have descended to the surface of the earth at my command;
having been born into all various castes, they shall once again be devoted to the worship of the Liṅga.
Having established themselves in the rank of Uttara-Vīra-Śaivas for the welfare of men in the world,
they shall wander about bearing the five mudrās, and at the end, they will come to me.
Whenever there occurs a complete decline on the surface of the earth among those who possess the unity of Prāṇa and Śiva,
At those various times, the lords of the Gaṇas, having been born into the mortal race, indeed establish the dharma. || 23 ||
The feet of the Guru, which remove worldly existence, which are the ornament for the heart of those seeking refuge, and which bring about the bliss of the Self.
I praise that which provides deliverance from the fear of death and which obstructs the rays of the young, rising sun. || 24 ||
O Three-eyed One, O Virūpākṣa, O Soma, O you who are adorned with the crescent moon!
O you whose three eyes are the three Vedas, whose eyes are the moon, the sun, and the fire! 25.
Salutations to you, O Lord of the deities; salutations to you of divine form.
Salutations to you, the Omniscient; salutations to the Lord of all beings. || 26 ||
In the *Skandapurāṇa*, Agastya said:
"Obeisance to Śiva, to the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*), and to the principle of knowledge (*vidyātattva*).”
To the one who is the reality of the self, who possesses both seedlessness and seed, and who is the source of the seed. || 27 ||
Salutations to the glorious Someśa Liṅga of Aipura, who exists in the form of the Liṅga.
Salutations to you, whose own form is the unity of the Liṅga and the body; salutations to you, the embodiment of the Liṅga.
In the word "Vātule," the sound "umā" is Umā herself, and the sound "śiva" is Śiva himself.
This word is the union of those two; we worship that Soma. || 29 ||
Śiva is the Liṅga and Umā is the body; thus, he is accompanied by her.
We worship these three words: "Soma," "Saṃbandha," and "Iti. || 30 ||
The Guru said:
Now, therefore, [I shall explain] the supreme method of instruction known as the Brahman of the six stations (ṣaṭsthalabrahma).
I shall explain in detail that which is born from the Śivasiddhāntatantra.
Just as it was previously taught and spoken by Śambhu, the Brahman of the Six Stages (Ṣaṭsthala).
The meaning taught to the Six-faced One is likewise stated here now.
In the *Vātula*, Pārvatī said: "O Lord, whose heart is moistened by compassion for me, I ask a question that brings victory."
O Mahādeva, speak to me that exposition of the Śivasiddhāntatantra; dispel my profound doubt.
Śiva said:
Well asked by you, O Goddess, this supreme question which brings joy to all.
I declare that to you as being of great significance, effecting liberation, and imperishable.

In this world of singular auspiciousness, dispassion causes happiness to depart, yet it does not remove suffering through its own lack of dispassion— how strange!
O Noble Jñānaśānta, having reflected upon this [teaching] which is not for the uninitiated, the Lord of the Pramathas should instill it within his own being. || 35 ||
And this, which is more secret than the secret, must not be given to just anyone.
O high-minded one, for the detached disciple who serves with devotion, [this is intended]. (36)
In the Vātula, it is said: "This tantra is not to be disclosed; it is a secret, exceedingly difficult to obtain."
I shall now briefly expound the great tantra of the knowledge of Śiva.
This tantra, the compendium of all scriptures, is more secret than the secret.
More subtle than the subtle, the essence of essences, it is the supreme source of great prosperity.
And by means of the Śruti, Smṛti, and Itihāsas, as well as the scriptures such as the Śivadharmas.
The Śivasiddhāntatantra, which provides a definitive exposition on the six locations (ṣaṭsthala), is now being told.
By means of the Śiva-āgamas, which contain the secrets of the non-duality of Śiva and are ultimate in nature.
The Śivasiddhāntatantra, which provides a definitive exposition on the six stages (ṣaṭsthala), is now being told.
By all the Upaniṣadic statements and by the Purāṇas whose purpose is the higher truth.
The Śivasiddhāntatantra, which provides a definitive determination of the six locations (ṣaṭsthala), is now being told.
And by all the essences of songs [composed] by the ancient great-minded ones.
The Śivasiddhāntatantra, which provides a definitive exposition on the six locations (ṣaṭsthala), is now being told.
Through the teacher’s instruction, through one's own experience, through reasoning, and through valid means of knowledge.
The Śivasiddhāntatantra, which provides a definitive exposition on the six locations (ṣaṭsthala), is now being told.
The meter is Vṛtta.
Through the experience of the grace obtained from the unsurpassed compassion of these three— the Guru, the Lord’s feet, and the form of Śiva—
I have spoken this supreme and most secret treasure, which is endowed with the meaning of the profound dialogue between the illustrious Teacher and his foremost disciple. 44.
Having respectfully extracted the very essence of all these meanings, [I shall compose this work].
I shall briefly expound the Śivasiddhāntatantra as spoken by Śiva.
The meter is Vṛtta.
Having joyfully prostrated at the lotus feet of the preeminent bull among devotees,
the king of yogis known as Siddhavīraṇa, the foremost of the Vīraśaivas, [spoke].
I compose this compendium of the essence of the Anādivīraśaiva tradition, which is praised by the Śruti and Smṛti, and which is a compendium of the essence of the primordial song. 46.
The names of the twenty-seven locations;
now, therefore, in this excellent compendium of the essence of Anādī Vīraśaivism:
The locations here are declared to be of twenty-seven varieties.
First is the Pīṭhikāsūtra, which is beginningless and characterized by devotion.
The second is the supreme, mobile land, which is devoid of a beginning.
One should know the third as the site of the Śūnya-liṅga, and the fourth likewise.
The fifth is said to be the location of the Liṅga known as Niṣkala. || 49 ||
The sixth is Mahāliṅgasthala, which possesses a liṅga in the form of the Praṇava.
The seventh is the place of universal birth; the eighth is now declared. || 50 ||
The ninth is the Piṇḍasthala, and the tenth is the Piṇḍacitsthala.
The eleventh stage, which pertains to that portion of saṃsāra to be abandoned, has been illustrated. || 51 ||
The twelfth [practice], the wearing of the liṅga, should be known as consisting of the compassion of the Guru.
The thirteenth is the greatness of the guide, and the fourteenth is [the greatness of the disciple]. || 52 ||
The fifteenth is the greatness of one's own chosen liṅga (sveṣṭaliṅgamāhātmya), and the sixteenth shall be [the next].
The seventeenth [chapter] shall be endowed with the majesty of the Caraliṅga.
And the greatness of serene faith is said to consist of eighteen aspects.
And the greatness of the water for washing the feet is proclaimed in the ninth and tenth [chapters]. || 54 ||
The greatness of sacred ash and the significance of rudrākṣa beads are recorded as twenty.
The twenty-one-fold [recitation] is renowned for the greatness of the five-syllabled mantra. || 55 ||
The site of the devotee (Bhaktasthala) and the site of Maheśvara (Māheśvarasthala) shall consist of twenty-two [parts].
It is declared to be twenty-three, joined with twenty-four.
In this very place, the Prasādisthala is proclaimed to consist of twenty-five [parts].
The Prāṇaliṅgisthala is said to consist of twenty-six [parts] here.
The place of refuge for unity is the twenty-seventh station.
I shall now demonstrate the path of the creative activity of consciousness for these [beings]. (58)
The Pīṭhikāsūtra.
If it is asked how the *Anādivīraśaiva-Ṣaṭsthalajñānasārasaṃgrahaparikrama* proceeds, [the answer is found in] the *Pīṭhikāsūtra*:
"The entire universe, situated within the universe, is contained within the womb of the mass that constitutes the vessel of the entire glorious Brahmāṇḍa..."

The beginningless Supreme Śiva— who is partless, without support, free from disease, without dependence, void of emptiness, stainless, eternal, and consisting of perfect existence, consciousness, and bliss—
having brought about the cessation of the three sections associated with the path of the world’s conventional activity and the creative will of Māyā;

Having established the essence of the six-fold knowledge of Anādivīraśaiva— consisting of the states of inherent nature (*svābhāvika*), action (*karma*), devotion (*bhakti*), and knowledge (*jñāna*)— Śambhu himself became known as the Guru in order to make even those who were previously bound attain the state of eternal liberation within a single lifetime.
To that good guru, whose true name is "Excellent Knowledge" (Sujñāna) because he was born from the lotus of divine knowledge and bliss,

his disciple made this representation while being one who finds happiness in union with the six-fold Brahma-aṅga-linga through the gaze of the compassionate side-long glance of his venerable teacher: "O good guru, by the sight of your compassionate glance, [I have become] happy in the union with the six-fold Brahma-aṅga-linga."
"Having become so, I am immediately liberated. "O Sadguro, beyond this, one doubt still appears to me;
out of compassion, do not abandon me, who am possessed of this doubt, but resolve my uncertainty.
When asked how that may be, some who abide in the Śaiva philosophy [replied as follows]..."
Regarding the determination of the pedestal, the thread, and the site: they speak of Vīraśaiva, Anādiśaiva, Pūrvavīraśaiva, and Uttaraśaiva.

When it was said, "Having ascertained its various divisions, please explain them in such a way that all doubt may be removed," that teacher, whose form is the Reality, being greatly delighted, replied: "O disciple, the question you have asked is beneficial to all the world; knowing this, those who are devoted to the Guru and detached from worldly things [should listen]."

Having attained the state of supreme bliss that is inherently partless, so that one may become eternally happy, we shall speak the essence of the knowledge of the six sites (ṣaṭsthala) of Anādivīraśaiva; listen with a steady mind.
From this point forward, considering that the words of Śiva state that Vīraśaivism is the most excellent,

whether one is called "Anādiparaśiva" or "Vīraśaiva endowed with the knowledge and practice of the union between the Liṅga and the Aṅga," having himself become the reality of the Great Liṅga (Mahāliṅgatattva), he himself [is] that treasure of the Great Liṅga.

Having become twofold, assuming the forms of the mobile beings born from the division of the *liṅga* and the *aṅga*, and having worshipped itself as both the worshipper and the worshipped, it became the beginningless, supreme, and non-dual Vīraśaivism. By that means, through the great *liṅga* which is without parts, the Supreme Power (*paraśakti*), the Supreme Sound (*paranāda*), the Point (*bindu*), and the digit (*kalā*) became one.

From that Sadāśiva, who is the embodiment of Sadāśiva himself, the five sages beginning with Gautama were initiated by means of his five faces; this constitutes the determination of the six Śaiva systems— namely Ādiśaiva, Mahāśaiva, and so forth—
as well as the Pīṭhikā, Sūtra, and Sthala sections.
Furthermore, those called Śaiva and Pāśupata are said to be the six Śaiva systems;

namely, the three Śaiva systems consisting of Pūrvaśaiva, Mārgaśaiva, and Śuddhaśaiva. Thus, these fifteen kinds of Śaiva systems exist as belonging to Sadāśiva, arising from the form of that Sadāśiva.
Among the five faces and the five *sādākhya*s, only the four beginning with the *kartṛ* (the agent) are *niṣkala* (partless);
the *karma-sādākhya* alone is *sakala* (with parts). That very *karma-sādākhya* became the form of Maheśvara, whose nature consists of twenty-five guileless (*nirguṇa*) divine sports (*līlā*).
From the face, arms, and thighs of that form of Maheśvara, Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā were born; indeed,
these three forms became the six philosophical systems (ṣaḍdarśana) and other doctrines among the Vaiṣṇava, Śaiva, and other Vedāntins, such that Vīraśaivism alone [prevails] through its few rituals.

He will lead his own people to dense liberation (*ghanamukti*), whereas [those following] Śaivism with its many rituals will attain only a small fruit; those who rely on other paths remain after experiencing various humiliations while their views are being scrutinized.
Therefore, the answer is always that one should take refuge in the six-fold station (*ṣaṭsthala*) of Vīraśaiva alone from time immemorial.

That which is free from birth, existence, and death belongs to the Śaiva system alone; other systems, such as the Sāṃkhya and others, are possessed of beginning and end, and for this reason they are called "ancient" (pūrva). Since their own liberation does not occur, those [other] Śaiva systems remain within the realm of worldly existence (bhava);
this is a great point of contention and is not merely a matter of words.
This *Pīṭhikāsūtrasthalanirūpaṇa*, the knowledge of the six stations (*ṣaṭsthalajñāna*) of beginningless Vīraśaivism, was expounded by Mahādeva to Umā and Skanda;
it is the essence of the four Vedas, the thirty-two Upaniṣads, the eighteen Smṛtis, and the twenty-eight Āgamas.

Saying, "Listen to this," which has been perfectly composed by ancient Pramatha hosts such as Bhṛṅgiriṭi, Ghaṇṭākarṇa, Sukeśa, Ruru, Upamanyu, Bhṛgu, Dadhīci, Gautama, and other sages, as well as in the Purāṇas, Itihāsas, and other works; he spoke thus.

The venerable Guru, whose form is the essence of existence, purity, and bliss, extracted the essential texts from all the Vedas, Āgamas, Purāṇas, Śāstras, the *Śivarahasya*, and other works, and compiled them into twenty-seven sacred sites (*sthala*).
If one asks how this was done, it is like a large elephant appearing as if dissolved within a small mirror. In these [twenty-seven sites], [the truth is thus revealed].
In the subtle stages, one hundred and one stages remain dissolved;
this essence of the knowledge of the six stages of Anādivīraśaivism remains together with twenty-seven stages, as they truly are, within those [subtle stages].
The twenty-six stages, beginning with the stage of the uninitiated devotee (*anādibhakta*) and ending with the stage of oneness (*aikya*),
together with the stage of the exposition of the Vīraśaiva injunctions (*vīraśaivanirdeśavivaraṇa*), constitute twenty-seven stages in total.

In the first [chapter], there is the exposition and commentary on Vīraśaiva: the Guru is indeed the partless (niṣkala), the Liṅga is indeed the void (śūnya), and the mobile and immobile (jaṅgama) is indeed the stainless (nirañjana). These—the Guru, the Liṅga, and the Jaṅgama—are themselves the forms of the gross, subtle, and causal bodies. He who is devoted from beginningless time is this very one, the one devoted from beginningless time.

Having realized that the great reality, which is the very nature of one’s own body, life-force, and consciousness, cannot be served [by another], he himself, through his own divine play, became twofold;
and out of reverence to worship himself by himself, he himself manifested as the threefold form consisting of the Guru, the Liṅga, and the Jaṅgama.

Having become manifest of its own accord, the partless Guru himself became the Sound (nāda); the Void-Liṅga itself became the Drop (bindu); and that which is born of the beginningless mobile world became the Energy (kalā). Thus, endowed with this Sound, Drop, and Energy, it became the Great Liṅga, a mass of splendor in the form of an undivided sphere.
That very Mahāliṅga became a Vīraśaiva, whose body was united with the six-fold Liṅgas as its constituent parts.
If it is asked, "How is that so?"
By the word *vi* is meant *yukti* (reasoning), and by the word *ra*, the notion of *rajas* (passion).
By the syllable *va* the *bindu* is indicated, and by the syllable *śa* consciousness (*cit*) is expressed. || 1 ||

Just as the word *siṃha* is derived from the verbal root *hiṃs* through the transposition of letters, so too the word *śiva* is derived from the verbal root *vaś*, meaning "to desire," through the transposition of letters. *Śiva* itself is *Śaiva*;
here the suffix *aṇ* is used in its own sense (*svārthe*). Furthermore, the letter *śa* is the *liṅga* in the form of a fixed sphere (*kūṭastha-golaka*) and also the form of the devotee.

Because it has been stated thus, the very seed-syllable consisting of the four letters *vī-va-ś-e* became known by the name "Vīraśaiva" once one has become a devotee of the *liṅga*. If it is asked how that [seed-syllable] can be the five-syllabled *praṇava*, the abode of the six-syllabled [mantra], and yet devoid of the inscription of even a single syllable, [the answer is: "The *liṅga* is the form of the five-syllabled [mantra]."
Because of the scriptural statement that the devotee is of the single form of six syllables, [it follows] that the *liṅga* is indeed five-syllabled.
The Examination of the Platform, the Sūtra, and the Ground.
The Lord said: "O Goddess, the syllable Oṃ is the face; the two words 'namas' are the two arms."
The letter Śa is the middle of the body, while the two letters Vāyau constitute the two feet.

"Thus, the form of the six syllables and the form of devotion have been declared by me. By this [statement], it is shown that while there are fifty-two syllables in the six-syllabled mantra, the *praṇava* beyond these syllables is indeed the "speechless" (*avāk*).
In this way, the five-syllabled, six-syllabled, and single-syllabled [mantras] are themselves the seals (*mudrās*) of the three principles (*tattvas*), the self, the movement, and the supreme.
If it is asked, "How was it that [the world], having been one alone without a second, became Vīraśaiva Brahman? [the answer follows]. || 90 ||
In the *Uttaravātula*:
"That which is the supreme state, non-conceptual, one alone and without a second."
That is called Vīraśaiva; it is not the other [type], which is characterized by conceptual construction (savikalpaka).
He who is this one alone within this entire world.
Because he moves with distinction, he is therefore called "Vīra" (the Hero). || 92 ||
Īśvara said: There is one form with three divisions: the Guru, the Liṅga, and the Jaṅgama.
The mobile Guru is also a Liṅga; thus, the Liṅga is said to be threefold.
In the *Bindūpaniṣad*, it is said:
"The Guru is indeed the mobile liṅga, whose form consists of nāda, bindu, and kalā."
The Nāda is known as the form of the Guru, while the Bindu is the form of the Liṅga.
That which moves in the form of *kalā* is to be known as that which is described in all the scriptures. || 94 ||
Īśvara said:
Nāda is indeed the mouth of the Guru, and likewise, bindu is the mouth of the liṅga.
The digit (kalā) is to be known as the face of Śiva, while the Guru is the mobile liṅga. || 95 ||
Nāda is to be known as the liṅga, and bindu is declared to be the pīṭha.
The form associated with the bindu and nāda is here said to be in the shape of a liṅga.
The proof for this is as follows.
The previously mentioned distinction of Śiva into the states of *laya* and so forth pertains indeed to his limiting adjunct (*upādhi*).
That is to be understood as the Bindu; she herself is considered to be Kuṇḍalinī.
That which is the supreme state for those who have reached the ultimate limit of leading others to nirvāṇa.
Then those solely intent on the knowledge of Śiva declare that place to be non-duality.
The Supreme Brahman alone is one, characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss.

These, having been cut and crushed, should be gently winnowed and prepared.

They undergo transformation through the sixfold division of nutriment.

Eatable food, soft food, drink, that which is to be licked, that which is to be sucked, and thick liquid.

And that food was eaten by embodied beings in the form of coarse morsels and mouthfuls.
